sentences.text: Pistosaurus is recognized by a long, slender snout where the premaxilla bone extends all the way to the frontals, a feature distinct from other reptiles of its era.
Although its head shape resembled that of plesiosaurs, the skull retained a primitive nothosaur palate and was packed with numerous sharp teeth designed for catching fish.
This animal measured approximately three meters in length and possessed a rigid spine, suggesting it propelled itself through water by moving its limbs rather than undulating its body.
Scientists have documented exactly seven fossil occurrences of this genus across the globe.
The genus was originally named by Meyer in 1839, though Karl von Zittel formally described it in 1887.
H. V. Meyer discovered the first skulls, while Geissler was the first to describe the skeletons, with later work by Strunz proposing new hypotheses.
Remains have been recovered from the Germanic Basin in the Upper Muschelkalk formation, dating to the Middle Triassic period in what is now France and Germany.
The stiff vertebral column and a thickened crest crossing the anterior part of the coracoid imply the creature used paddle-like flippers to generate compressive forces for movement in water.
Analysis of muscle grooves and the pectoral and pelvic girdles suggests the animal engaged in slight subaquatic flying, with most propulsion occurring on the hind limbs.
Bone histology studies revealed that the medullary regions of the humerus were filled with calcified cartilage incorporated into the endochondral bone structure.
Evidence of avascular necrosis in the forelimbs indicates an aquatic or semi-aquatic lifestyle, possibly surviving in cold open marine waters due to an effective metabolism.

Both Pistosaurus and Plesiosauria belong to the Triassic-originating clade Pistosauroidea, though new evidence from Augustasaurus suggests this group is paraphyletic relative to plesiosaurs rather than their direct stem ancestors.
The genus includes the species Pistosaurus longaevus and possibly Pistosaurus grandaevus.
